items.text: Major infrastructure, such as power grids and railways, should be built according to one coordinated long-term plan.
items.rationale: Social democrats, developmental-state nationalists and socialists endorse planned networks; market liberals prefer competing providers. Ownership-neutral; reads in both frames.

items.text: What the economy produces should be decided mainly by a deliberate plan rather than by what sells at a profit.
items.rationale: Core planner claim (state socialists, participatory-planning anarchists, some religious economists); strong but fair. Ideal vs here-and-now may split on feasibility.

items.text: Investment in key industries should be steered toward publicly chosen goals, even when investors would put the money elsewhere.
items.rationale: Directed investment: industrial-policy advocates, dirigistes, East Asian developmentalists, green planners. Says nothing about who owns the firms.

items.text: If the price of a basic necessity like housing or medicine soars, it should be capped.
items.rationale: Plan-favouring condition (price spike); rent-control and price-cap supporters across left and populist right endorse. Plausible frame split.

items.text: Large firms should have to meet production and investment targets set by an economy-wide plan.
items.rationale: Strong planning (Soviet-style or indicative-planning hardliners, corporatists); firms may be private or public, so ownership-independent.

items.text: If markets fail to supply enough of something people need, such as housing, it should be produced according to a plan.
items.rationale: Plan-favouring condition (market failure); mainstream left and pragmatic conservatives endorse. Works hypothetically in both frames.

items.text: If competing firms waste resources duplicating each other's products, production in that industry should be coordinated under a single plan.
items.rationale: Classic socialist and technocratic critique of competitive waste, stated as adherents put it; plan-favouring condition.

items.text: Most prices should be whatever buyers and sellers freely agree on.
items.rationale: Baseline market claim held by liberals, conservatives, market socialists and libertarians; agentless, reads in both frames.

items.text: Even the prices of essentials like food and rent should be set by buyers and sellers alone.
items.rationale: Strong market pole mirroring pla-04; classical liberals and libertarians endorse. Frames may split where caps exist today.

items.text: Money for new projects should go wherever investors expect the best returns, rather than to goals picked by planners.
items.rationale: Mirror of pla-03; market liberals and Austrian-school adherents endorse. 'Investors' may be private, cooperative or public funds.

items.text: Businesses that lose out to competitors should be allowed to close, even large ones that many jobs depend on.
items.rationale: Strong pro-competition/no-bailout view (libertarians, Schumpeterian liberals); thoughtful people may answer differently here-and-now vs ideal.

items.text: If price limits cause shortages, prices should be left free to find the level where supply meets demand.
items.rationale: Market-favouring condition (shortages from caps); economists of most stripes and market advocates endorse; hypothetical reading works where no caps exist.

items.text: If officials' bets on chosen industries keep failing, investment decisions should be left to investors competing for returns.
items.rationale: Market-favouring condition (failed industrial policy); liberals and public-choice sceptics endorse. Ownership-neutral.

items.text: If a disaster causes shortages, prices should be allowed to rise so that more supply is drawn in.
items.rationale: Strong market view (opposition to anti-gouging rules) as free-market economists state it; mirrors pla-04's cap logic at the hard end.
